proposal: The Mandate calls marketing orders and checkoff programs compelled-funding arrangements and recommends that USDA reduce their number and scope, reject new requests where the law allows, eliminate existing programs when possible, make it easier for affected parties to end them, and reject any return of volume controls. It also recommends working with Congress to eliminate them, or at least to require a vote of affected parties at least every five years that USDA must honor.
remaining: A general USDA effort to reduce the number and scope of checkoff programs and marketing orders and to reject new requests (p. 306): the 2026-09-17 directive limits one category of checkoff spending (ESG commitments) across programs but does not reduce their number; the terminations and withdrawals found followed producer votes under existing statutes, and several AMS actions (Christmas tree expense cap, proposed South Texas onion amendments) went the other way at industry request.

Easier termination and a USDA duty to honor termination requests (p. 306): none found; the South Texas onion proposal would lower the share needed to continue that order, which is the reverse direction.

Legislation to eliminate marketing orders and checkoffs or to require votes at least every five years (p. 306): none found; the checkoff bills found (H.R. 3516, S. 1848) are transparency and lobbying bills.
Volume controls (p. 306): a marketing order with supply regulation, spearmint oil, was still being implemented in 2026.

status_summary: On 2026-09-17 USDA announced an end to dairy checkoff support for the Innovation Center for U.S. Dairy's ESG-related projects and directed AMS to ensure that no research and promotion funds in other commodity checkoffs advance ESG mandates; the release describes returning the programs to their core mission and does not reduce their number, reject new requests, ease termination or require votes. The reductions in the number of programs found came from producer-initiated processes under existing law: AMS terminated the paper and paper-based packaging order in a final rule published 2026-03-09 after a 2025 referendum favoring termination, and withdrew the proposed natural grass sod order on 2025-05-29 after producers rejected it. Other AMS actions went the other way at industry request, including a Christmas tree order amendment raising the board's expense cap (effective 2026-04-08) and a January 2026 hearing notice on South Texas onion order amendments that would lower the continuance threshold, while the House-passed farm bill (H.R. 7567) extends the dairy checkoff through 2031. The 119th Congress checkoff bills found (H.R. 3516 and S. 1848) address lobbying, conflicts of interest, transparency and audits, with no termination or periodic-vote provision in the House text.

timeline.event: Rep. Mace introduces H.R. 3516, the Opportunities for Fairness in Farming Act of 2025 (Sen. Lee's companion, S. 1848, was introduced 2025-05-21): it would bar large checkoff boards from contracting with groups that seek to influence agricultural policy, ban conflicts of interest and anticompetitive conduct, and require budget publication and audits; the House text has no referendum or termination provision.

AMS publishes a direct final rule removing 7 CFR part 1240, the referendum procedures for the proposed Natural Grass Sod Promotion, Research, and Information Order, after producers voted against the order (36.49 percent in favor); the rule calls itself deregulatory under Executive Order 14192 and the proposed order is withdrawn through a separate notice.

AMS publishes a rule on the Paper and Paper-Based Packaging Promotion, Research and Information Order titled as a continuance referendum and moratorium on assessment collection; the later termination rule says this notice suspended assessment collection with immediate effect, after a petition from more than 10 percent of eligible voters in January 2025.

AMS publishes a hearing notice (hearing set for 2026-02-03 and 2026-02-04) on industry-submitted amendments to the South Texas onion order, including changing the continuance referendum threshold from two-thirds of voting producers to a majority and adding marketing promotion authority; an interim final rule effective 2026-05-26 later suspends the 2026 continuance referendum until 2032, citing the overlap with this rulemaking.

AMS publishes a final rule terminating the paper and paper-based packaging order and removing 7 CFR part 1222, effective the same day, after a referendum on 2025-07-14 to 2025-07-25 in which about 73.5 percent of voters (about 90.4 percent of volume) favored ending it; the order had taken effect 2014-01-23 and collected about $21.2 million from 46 entities in 2024.

AMS publishes a final rule (effective 2026-04-08) amending the Christmas tree promotion order at the board's recommendation: the administrative expense cap rises from 10 to 15 percent, the board is renamed, and meeting and records rules change; the rule is exempt from Executive Order 14192.

The House passes H.R. 7567 (224 to 200); per CRS, it extends the National Dairy Promotion and Research Board's authority, which expires 2026-09-30 under current law, through 2031-09-30, and the Senate bill reauthorizes the dairy checkoff with minor wording differences.

AMS publishes notice of a second Christmas tree order continuance referendum (voting 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-16, about 1,200 eligible persons) because the May to June 2026 vote showed 49.83 percent support and had a shortened window with late ballots; if a majority does not favor continuing, USDA would follow the order's suspension and termination procedures.

USDA announces an end to dairy checkoff funding of the Innovation Center for U.S. Dairy's ESG-related projects and directs AMS to ensure that no research and promotion funds in other commodity checkoffs advance ESG mandates; the release does not reduce the number of programs or change termination or voting rules.
